input: If we let students submit one assignment late, soon nobody will meet deadlines, teachers will lose control, and the school year will become chaos.
label: fallacy
rationale: It predicts a chain from one exception to widespread disorder without evidence that each step will follow.

input: If the café lets one customer bring a small dog inside, next people will bring large dogs, then farm animals, and eventually the café will become a zoo.
label: fallacy
rationale: Allowing a small dog does not automatically justify allowing every other animal; reasonable limits could distinguish the cases.

input: The city is considering adding one speed bump. If we accept that, we might as well put speed bumps on every street until nobody can drive anywhere.
label: fallacy
rationale: It assumes one speed bump will lead to unlimited additions without explaining why the city would keep adding them.

input: If a five-minute extension is acceptable, why not ten minutes, then an hour, then let everyone submit work whenever they want?
label: fallacy
rationale: Accepting a small extension does not mean larger extensions must also be accepted; each limit can have a reason.

input: If the library starts lending laptops, people will ask to borrow tablets too, then phones, and soon the library will have to lend every item anyone requests.
label: fallacy
rationale: Lending laptops does not establish a rule that the library must lend every requested item; it can set eligibility and inventory limits.

input: If I order takeout tonight, I'll order it every night this week, stop cooking entirely, and waste all my money on food.
label: fallacy
rationale: It treats one takeout meal as inevitably leading to repeated ordering and financial harm without supporting those links.

input: If the company allows employees to work from home on Fridays, they may request more remote days, so management should decide in advance how requests will be handled.
label: not_fallacy
rationale: It anticipates a plausible follow-up request and proposes a policy, without claiming that an extreme outcome is inevitable.

input: If you leave an ice cube in direct sunlight on a warm day, it will melt.
label: not_fallacy
rationale: This is a simple, well-established causal prediction, not an unsupported chain of escalating consequences.

input: The restaurant is thinking of raising its prices by 5%. If 5% is acceptable, then 6% must be acceptable, and eventually customers will have to accept any price.
label: fallacy
rationale: A small price increase does not imply that every larger increase is justified; the argument treats a gradual change as if no meaningful limit exists.

input: If we miss the last train, we will need to take a taxi home, because the timetable shows that no more trains run tonight.
label: not_fallacy
rationale: The consequence follows from a stated timetable and is limited and plausible, rather than an unsupported slide toward an extreme.
